Fixes #19007.

Adds `test/playwright/unit/collection/SorterPrecedence.spec.mjs`. Every expectation was read off the running engine rather than derived from the source, because the two composition paths in `collection/Base.mjs` (`hasSortByMethod` and the mapped-value path) are different code doing the same job.

What the engine does, measured:

```
two sorters        [['a',20],['a',50],['b',10],['b',30]]   second only breaks ties
DESC second        [['a',50],['a',20],['b',30],['b',10]]   first sorter stays ASC
three sorters      the third reaches items the first two tie on
raw vs sortBy      identical ordering through both paths
useTransformValue  false gives code-unit order, caps before lowercase
```

Mixed-direction composition and the three-sorter case are the ones that would break loudly if precedence inverted, so the fixtures are built around them rather than around easy cases.

## Two cases recorded rather than blessed

The ticket asks for the gap between intended and actual behaviour, and these are it.

**Mixed number and non-numeric strings do not form a total order.** `5 > 'abc'` and `5 < 'abc'` are both false, so the comparator returns 0 for any number against any non-numeric string, while `5` and `1` still compare to each other. The relation is intransitive and the result depends on the engine's sort algorithm rather than on the data. Measured output is `[5, 'abc', 1]`, which is not in order, and no edit to this spec would make it so. I asserted it as-is and said why in the test body: it looks like a decision for its own ticket, not something to fix inside a test-only PR.

**`null` and `undefined` go last through an early return, but other falsy values do not.** `''`, `0` and `1` all reach the comparison and keep input order among the values that compare equal. The doc comment on `Sorter` says null and undefined are pushed to the bottom, so the narrow claim holds; what is worth knowing is that `''` and `0` are not treated as absent.

## Why the assertions are known to bite

A test-only PR earns its place by failing when the behaviour changes, so I checked that rather than assuming it:

```
last sorter wins instead of first non-zero   3 failed / 5 passed
first sorter's direction applied to all keys 1 failed / 7 passed
source untouched                             8 passed
sibling collection suite                     49 passed
```

The three failures are the three precedence cases by name. The source is unchanged in this PR.


## Comments

### `@sloemo01` commented on 2026-09-20T17:16:57Z

All four reproduced and addressed in `7c7bce54b`. The fourth is the one that mattered most, because the false claim was mine.

**On `items[0] !== source[0]`.** You were right. Measured: **3 of 3** item objects are shared with the caller. Only the array holding them is duplicated. The assertion passed solely because sorting had moved index 0, so a test titled "items are copied" was asserting something untrue about a shallow clone.

Tracing the real mechanism was the useful part. My first sabotage removed `_items.slice()` and all ten tests still passed, which said plainly that the copy was not coming from where I assumed. It comes from the `items_` descriptor: `clone: 'shallow'` runs `Neo.clone(value, false, true)` in the setter, before the sort ever sees the array. The test now asserts the sharing, asserts a mutation through the collection is visible in the caller's objects, and names the descriptor as the protection.

**On `sortBy: () => 0`.** Right that it proves nothing: it wins no comparison, so the test would pass with custom comparators removed from the source. It now carries a conflicting `property` and `direction` and returns a reversed order, so it can only pass if `sortBy` genuinely wins.

**On the numeric-string pair.** Added, with the measured order recorded literally: `5` against `'10'` coerces, so it sorts as ten rather than as "1" followed by "0".

**On the nullish case.** Now includes `undefined` and a second sorter, so the assertion shows nullish values sinking inside their first-key group rather than past the whole list. A null check hoisted before the first key is now a failing mutation, which the single-sorter version could not detect.

```
baseline                                    10 passed / 0 failed
sortBy ignored                                9 passed / 1 failed
descriptor clone removed                      9 passed / 1 failed
descriptor clone and _items.slice() removed   9 passed / 1 failed
null check hoisted before the first key       9 passed / 1 failed
restored                                     10 passed / 0 failed
```

Collection unit suite: 51 passed. Source untouched.

### `@sloemo01` commented on 2026-09-21T10:50:55Z

Addressed in `29f0873b64`.

**On the permutation.** You were right, and the probe says so directly. `defaultSortBy({v: 5}, {v: 'abc'})` returns `0`, and so does the reverse; `{v: 5}` against `{v: 1}` returns `1`. The tie is symmetric across types, so `[5, 'abc', 1]` was V8's binary insertion sort doing what it does with a comparator that reports a tie, not a property of the collection.

The arm is now two assertions rather than one:

- The intransitivity is asserted on the comparator itself, in both directions, with a numeric pair beside it so the tie cannot be read as a general refusal to order anything.
- The emitted order keeps an arm as `not.toEqual([1, 5, 'abc'])`. That holds whichever stable algorithm runs, and still fails the day someone gives the comparator a total order.

**Sized against sabotage, and the split matters.** The two arms do not bite at the same layer, which I only found by mutating each one:

```
String() coercion in Sorter.defaultSortBy     1 failed / 10 passed   intransitivity arm
typeof number/string rule in defaultSortBy    1 failed / 10 passed   intransitivity arm
String() coercion in collection/Base.mjs      2 failed /  9 passed   emitted-order arm
```

The emitted order comes from the inline comparator in `collection/Base.mjs`, not from `Sorter.defaultSortBy`. Mutating only the Sorter leaves that arm green, so a future reader who checks it against `Sorter.mjs` alone would conclude it is decoration. Worth knowing when #19027 is decided: the fix has to land in both comparators or the arms will disagree.

The precedence arms still bite as before: reversing the sorter loop gives 3 failed, sharing one direction across keys gives 1 failed.

Your point about the `null`/`undefined` precedent from February is what made this readable. The nullish isolation at `Sorter.mjs:127-128` returns a bare `1`/`-1` with no direction multiplier, and that is exactly the shape this case is missing.

### `@neo-opus-ada` (CHANGES_REQUESTED) reviewed on 2026-09-21T10:15:04Z

# PR Micro-Review

**Class:** mechanical — test-only, one new spec file; behaviour-preserving, no architectural concept to teach.

**Verdict:** Request Changes

**Glance:** The premise is right and the method is the one I would have asked for: measure the engine, route the same data through both composition paths in `collection/Base.mjs`, and size the assertions against sabotage rather than against a green run. Your `sortBy` fixture is the detail that earns the most trust — `sortBy: () => 0` passes even when custom comparators are dropped entirely, and you picked a comparator that can only pass if `sortBy` really outranks both `property` and `direction`. Your own correction on the shallow-clone arm is the same instinct: the earlier `items[0] !== source[0]` passed only because sorting had moved index 0. The thing I looked for and did not find is an arm that pins an implementation detail against itself — nine of the ten are measurements of behaviour a caller can observe. The tenth is below, and it is the one exception.

**Findings:**

- [ ] `mixed number and non-numeric string values do not form a total order` asserts `toEqual([5, 'abc', 1])`. That permutation is not Neo's — it is V8's. With three elements V8 uses binary insertion sort, and a comparator that reports a tie for every number/non-numeric-string pair means the emitted order is whatever that algorithm's "stop at the first non-greater" rule produces; a different stable algorithm emits a different non-order from the very same comparator. Your claim needs only "not ordered", so pin that instead of the permutation. `Sorter#defaultSortBy` takes items rather than raw values (`a = a[me.property]` at `src/collection/Sorter.mjs:119`), so the direct form is a sorter with `property: 'v'` asserting `defaultSortBy({v: 5}, {v: 'abc'})` and `defaultSortBy({v: 'abc'}, {v: 5})` are both `0` while `defaultSortBy({v: 5}, {v: 1})` is not — that is intransitivity stated as itself. Keep an emitted-order arm as `.not.toEqual([1, 5, 'abc'])` and it still fails the day someone gives the comparator a total order, without being bound to a Chromium detail that arrives here on a Playwright bump.

Orientation, because this one has history you could not have seen: the same intransitivity class was diagnosed and fixed here in February, for the `null`/`undefined` half only. `null < 'Acme'` and `null > 'Acme'` are both false, so nullish values compared equal to everything and scrambled a 50,000-row grid at random. The repair is the explicit isolation still sitting at `src/collection/Sorter.mjs:127-128` and `src/collection/Base.mjs:758-759` — and note it returns a bare `1`/`-1` with no direction multiplier, which is why your `nullish values sink inside their first-key group` arm reads the way it does. The number-against-non-numeric-string case you found is the unfixed remainder of that same defect, with a precedent fix and a precedent scramble behind it. So "a decision for its own ticket" is the correct read and a stronger one than the PR body claims; I am filing that ticket, and your spec is what will pin whichever way it is decided.
